Latest Update: Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.
  • Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

It has been revealed that with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

It has been revealed that every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

There is a newly introduced vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

Recent findings suggest that with a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

It has been revealed that delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

Industry observers note that we have a upcoming Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

Recent findings suggest that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Sources indicate that stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

In a recent development, susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and remarked Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”.

Wiles, who Trump recently revealed had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”.

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”.

Industry observers note that trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

According to recent reports, “Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”.

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

According to recent reports, miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

According to recent reports, virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

In a recent development, “Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer stated in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion demonstrates that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”.

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once noted the party is “unworthy of power.”.

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller mentioned during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

According to recent reports, for a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

And while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Deer were an vital source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

Industry observers note that roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

Winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn was one of the most vital foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively new to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

One traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

The waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

In a recent development, the English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

According to recent reports, squash and pumpkin were crucial crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

In a recent development, the English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in Newly introduced England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

It has been revealed that the Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous Latest England roots that remains an American favorite.

The forests and wetlands of Fresh England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

Nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

Industry observers note that of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

According to recent reports, sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie. I tested six to find out which one tasted the most homemade.

Sources indicate that planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook. There are many moving parts, and it can certainly be overwhelming when there is a houseful of hungry guests ready to dive into the biggest family meal of the year. That’s why I think there is no shame in turning to store-bought options for some elements of the meal. If baking isn’t your forte, but you still want to offer a traditional pumpkin pie for dessert, stores across the country are ready to help.

Industry observers note that I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the big day. The contenders are:.

It has been revealed that I sampled and ranked each one based on overall appearance, the flavor and texture of the crust, and, finally, the consistency of the filling and spices used. I was certainly surprised by my top choice.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Coming in at the bottom of my ranked list is the Bakeshop pumpkin pie from Aldi. This 8-inch pie is 1-1/2 pounds and costs $5.29. Before cutting a slice, I noticed that the crust on this pie was quite pale. So much so, I even checked the label to make sure I wasn’t expected to bake it before serving. When I took a bite, the taste was what I would expect from an undercooked crust. It was gummy and almost tasted raw. The filling was quite sweet, with the sugar, brown sugar and molasses flavors being the most prevalent and the pumpkin pie spices taking a backseat.

Bottom Line: The pumpkin pie from Aldi is a bargain at only $5.29, but the undercooked, super-sweet filling didn’t impress.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Selling for a bargain at $4.94, the pumpkin pie from Walmart was the least expensive pie I sampled. This 8-inch pie is 1 pound, 6 ounces. You might notice from the photograph that with this pie, the crust separated from the filling after cutting a slice. Sometimes this occurs when the custard is overcooked. Once again, I wasn’t impressed with the color of the crust and hoped for more browning and flavor. The filling also had a similar overly sweet taste that I noticed in the Aldi pie. I wish the spices in this pie were kicked up a notch or two as well.

Industry observers note that bottom Line: The price of a Walmart pumpkin pie can’t be beat, but the dessert isn’t the most flavorful of those I tested. Next time I might jazz it up with some spiced pecans just before serving.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

The pumpkin pie from Trader Joe’s was quite different from all the other pies in this sample group. Right out of the box, I noticed both the crust and the filling were a deep brown color. Quite a departure from some of the other anemic-looking pies. Selling for $6.99, this 9-inch pie is larger and heavier at 1 pound, 9.4 ounces. Reading the ingredient list, this pie included cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and allspice. As someone who loves these flavors, I couldn’t wait to dive in.

It has been revealed that this pie definitely didn’t hold back. The flavors are very bold, and the crust is well-browned. However, these spices are so bold that you almost lose the pumpkin’s flavor. This pie might have benefited from pulling back slightly on the spices to further highlight the star of the show, aka the pumpkin.

According to recent reports, bottom Line: If you like very bold pumpkin pie spices, this dessert from Trader Joe’s will fit the bill. However, the strong flavor might be divisive around the dinner table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that marie Callender’s is a brand known for pies, and you can pick up an unbaked pie in the freezer section of many grocery stores for a budget-friendly $5.97. It weighs 2 pounds, 4 ounces, and measures 8-1/2 inches across. There are both benefits and drawbacks to purchasing an unbaked pie. Since it’s kept frozen, there’s no need for a bunch of preservatives and fillers used in some of the shelf-stable pies I picked up at other stores. However, when you have to bake the pie yourself, there is room for user error and a risk of an overbaked or underbaked dessert.

Sources indicate that in terms of flavor and texture, this pie was middle-of-the-road across the board. The crust was good, it just wasn’t a showstopper that I’d be excited to bring to the table. I appreciated the creamy filling, but once again, I just wanted a more pumpkin-forward flavor.

Bottom Line: The flavor and texture of the Marie Callender’s crust was delightful, but it was not as visually appealing as some other store-bought options.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, at almost 2-1/2 pounds and 10 inches in diameter, the $7.99 pumpkin pie from Kroger (Mariano’s in my neck of the woods) was the largest of the pumpkin pies in this taste test. In addition, the perfectly fluted crust on this pie was lovely. It looked homemade and baked to perfection. The most prevalent flavor in the filling is cinnamon, with nutmeg, allspice and ginger lingering in the background. The pie cut well and sat nicely on the serving plate, but had a slightly gelatinous texture rather than a rich, creamy custard consistency. I would certainly buy this pie again, but next time I think I would kick it up a notch by serving with a bourbon whipped cream to really wow my guests.

Bottom Line: This was the most visually impressive pumpkin pie on the list and one that I’d be proud to present at the dessert table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

The pumpkin pie at my local Albertson’s (we call it Jewel in the Chicago area) is just shy of 8 inches wide and weighs 1 pound, 4 ounces for $7.99. Ultimately, in this taste test, this pie came closer to tasting homemade than any other option. This was the only pie I found that struck the ideal balance between warm fall spices and signature pumpkin flavor. I loved the prevalent cinnamon notes and the velvety texture of the filling. The crust was attractively presented and perfectly baked. It was actually the smallest of the pies I sampled and on the higher end in terms of price, but every bite was worth it.

Bottom Line: If I’m not making a homemade pumpkin pie this year, I’ll be relying on Albertson’s to do the work for me!

Sources indicate that which store-bought pie is your fave? Let us know in the comments below!

Sheet-Pan Cider Vinegar Chicken

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time.
  • Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp.
  • skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

More sheet-pan dinners this way.

Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

Scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

#88827. Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2016 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people.
  • Sources indicate that alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community.
  • Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Sources indicate that alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

According to recent reports, I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and strategy on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

It has been revealed that whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

According to recent reports, I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

Sources indicate that the first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

How about your latest kitchen adventure?

According to recent reports, I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have significant ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

In a recent development, my favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

What’s your most cherished cookbook?

It has been revealed that marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that showed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

Industry observers note that I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

It has been revealed that I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from New England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

It has been revealed that I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

Industry observers note that while my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was significant sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

The desk you work at may have more influence on productivity than you think, with research involving over 10,000 employees linking standing desks to greater daily computer activity.

In a recent development, for anyone who spends most of the workday in front of a computer, sitting for hours can leave the back aching, the neck stiff, and energy running low by midafternoon. Standing up and moving around can help break up that routine, which is part of the appeal of height-adjustable desks. These workstations let employees switch between sitting and standing without stepping away from their work, offering a simple way to reduce physical strain and spend less time in one position.

Industry observers note that now, a large study from Texas A&M University suggests that sit-stand desks may offer another advantage. Employees using them averaged about 43 more minutes of active computer use each day than those working at traditional desks. Over a year, that difference could represent nearly $9,000 in potential productivity value per employee.

Recent findings suggest that the research, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics, was co-led by Dr. Mark Benden, a professor at Texas A&M’s School of Public Health, and Dr. Tricia Salzar, Regional Ergonomist for the U.S. Army Public Health Command Region, West.

Sources indicate that rather than relying on a small laboratory experiment, the researchers examined how people used their computers during ordinary workdays. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk consumers and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden stated.

The team combined employee comfort surveys with software measurements of computer activity, including keystrokes, words typed, mouse clicks, and typing errors. This allowed the researchers to examine both how workers felt about their workstations and how actively they used their computers.

“It was key that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden said.

Employees with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time per day, compared with 2.95 hours among those using conventional desks. That difference of approximately 43 minutes may seem modest during a single workday, but the researchers calculated that it amounted to roughly 171 additional hours annually, equivalent to more than four 40-hour workweeks.

It has been revealed that the difference also extended beyond time spent using a computer. Employees with adjustable desks generally typed more words and recorded more keystrokes, suggesting that the additional activity was accompanied by greater measurable output.

“The data revealed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden said.

Using a standardized hourly wage of approximately $52, the researchers calculated that those 171 additional hours could represent nearly $9,000 in annual productivity value for each employee. The figure is an estimate based on computer activity and hourly wages, rather than a demonstrated increase in manufacturer profits or a financial return that accounts for the cost of purchasing the desks.

“Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden said.

The results are encouraging, although the comparison does not establish that the desks themselves caused the difference in activity. The measurements also do not directly show whether employees experienced less back pain, reduced fatigue, or better concentration. Those remain potential benefits rather than outcomes established by the reported computer-use findings.

In a recent development, still, the results add to a broader discussion about how the spaces people work in can influence their daily experience. Employers often look to new software, training, and management strategies to improve performance, while the physical surroundings receive less attention.

According to recent reports, “It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,’” Benden remarked. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.”.

According to recent reports, A sit-stand desk is a relatively straightforward example of that idea. Instead of requiring someone to remain seated throughout the day, it allows them to adjust their position as their comfort and tasks change. For workers who spend much of their time at a computer, that flexibility may make long workdays more manageable.

It has been revealed that “It can have a profound effect,” Benden noted. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.”.

Sources indicate that the possibility of easing physical discomfort while supporting more sustained energy and longer periods of focused work makes adjustable desks appealing to employees. For employers, the potential benefit is a workforce that can remain productive while working in a more comfortable environment.

“It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden stated.

Benden believes these findings demonstrate why workplace design deserves a larger role in conversations about employee health and organizational performance.

“The design of the workplace itself can be a powerful driver of human health and performance, including better engagement, productivity, and organizational success,” Benden mentioned.

“The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden stated. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance, and better organizational outcomes follow.”.

Understanding that relationship has been a major focus of Benden’s career. A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor, and internationally recognized researcher, he has spent decades investigating how work environments affect the people who use them.

Recent findings suggest that “We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden said. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.”.

He currently directs the Center for Worker Health at Texas A&M, which brings together engineering, management, and technology through interdisciplinary research, innovation, and education. Its work focuses on developing practical improvements in worker health and efficiency, while helping students turn their ideas into real-world applications.

In a recent development, “The Center partners with industry nationwide, to develop innovative, impactful systems and practices that have a direct effect on worker health and efficiency,” Benden said. “We also train students and give them the platform to be as creative as possible to turn latest ideas into impactful applications.”.

The research is also expanding beyond furniture and ergonomics. As artificial intelligence becomes a more common part of office work, Benden is interested in how these technologies might interact with the physical environments in which employees perform their jobs.

Sources indicate that “Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden stated. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.”.

For organizations considering changes to their offices, the findings suggest that improving the everyday experience of working at a computer may be worth examining alongside investments in new technology. Whether the goal is to reduce physical strain, encourage movement, or support productivity, even something as familiar as a desk could have a role to play.

“The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden said.

Sources indicate that reference: “Improved Computer Utilization Associated with Height Adjustable Workstations in a Large Office Population” by Tricia Lynn Salzar, Matthew Lee Smith, Adam Pickens, Gang Han and Mark Edward Benden, 19 September 2026, Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics. DOI: 10.3390/tae2030021.

Latest Update: 7 Simple Steps for Winterizing Your Lawn Mower

  • It has been revealed that winterizing is especially important for gas-powered mowers, which have engines that need fuel, oil, and an air filter to run properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Somehow the end of the year is upon us and mowing season is winding down. And while you should still be mowing your lawn until the first hard frost hits, soon it’ll be time to retire it for the winter, and you get to give that chore a rest for a bit. But you can’t just store the mower in the shed and forget about it. To ensure your lawn mower is ready to go next season, you need to winterize it before sending it into hibernation.

It has been revealed that winterizing is especially important for gas-powered mowers, which have engines that need fuel, oil, and an air filter to run properly. You should do some light maintenance on them before the cold weather arrives. While cordless electric lawn mowers are easier to maintain, there are still a few steps you should take before storing them away.

Industry observers note that here are our tips for winterizing any lawn mower so it’s ready to go in the spring. Note that you don’t have to do them in this exact order; for example, you might want to leave fuel stabilization until later in the process, but we wanted to keep it at the top, since it’s one of the most key steps.

In a recent development, prepping your gas-powered lawn mower for winter storage isn’t hard; there are just several things to consider, and if you cover them all, it should only take an hour or so. You will be dealing with engine fluids, however, so choose a work area and clothing that you don’t mind getting dirty.

According to recent reports, when left for long periods, gasoline can become “stale,” meaning it evaporates and oxidizes, making it less combustible. It can also create residues that could damage the engine. Also, the ethanol found in most gasoline can break down if left to sit, causing performance issues and attracting water that can cause corrosion (one of the reasons ethanol-free gas is better for lawn mowers).

Sources indicate that you can avoid the problems by adding a fuel stabilizer, but if there is any air in the tank, it’s not a perfect solution. Meanwhile, siphoning the gas from the tank is not truly going to remove all of it, so here’s our advice, in steps:.

Sources indicate that not everyone will recommend this method, but we believe that, since a full tank has almost no air in it, there is little space for fuel to evaporate or for condensation to form due to temperature changes. Therefore, you are less likely to encounter problems than if you had drained the tank.

Large gas-powered mowers, such as lawn tractors and zero-turn mowers, typically have a battery to power the starter, lights, and other accessories. Gas walk-behind mowers with an electric start feature will also have a battery. It’s a good idea to remove it for the winter and clean it to remove corrosion on the terminals or battery posts. When performing this task, wear nitrile gloves and eye protection. If your battery has a lot of corrosion, you don't want to remove it in a way that it gets airborne. You can use a solution of water and baking soda to neutralize the corrosion and wipe it off with a rag or microfiber cloth.

It has been revealed that most experts recommend replacing your spark plug every year. Changing your spark plug can vary depending on the model of lawn mower you own, so always consult your manual. If you do not feel it’s necessary to replace it, at least remove it to check for any damage. If you see a lot of carbon buildup, rust, or cracks, it’s best to change it.

In a recent development, drain the oil from the mower after letting it run for 5 minutes—warm oil flows more easily. For walk-behind mowers, this will require you to tip the mower over, so it’s probably better to remove the gas first or at least make sure the gas tank is securely sealed. When tipping the mower, the carburetor and air filter sections should be facing upward to avoid oil contamination—since the oil spout is usually on the opposite side of the carb and filter, you’ll naturally be following this rule anyway. But it’s good advice for when you tip the mower to clean the underside of the deck as well.

In a recent development, this is pretty easy to do, but it helps to know what the filter is made of. Paper and fiber filters should be replaced. If it’s a foam filter element, you can use water and Dawn dish soap, but make sure to rinse it well and let it air dry completely before reinstalling it.

Industry observers note that you should be cleaning your mower deck throughout the summer, but if not, make a point to do it before storing it; otherwise, the caked-on grass may cause corrosion or attract bugs and vermin. As mentioned above, make sure to tip your mower so that the air box and carburetor are on the high side to avoid fuel contamination.

After you’ve completed the task of cleaning the deck, it’s a good idea to wipe down your engine with a damp cloth, removing any dirt or debris, and dry it with another towel.

Industry observers note that the end of the season is a good time to sharpen your mower blade or replace it altogether. You can take it to a lawn mower repair shop to have it done, but if you have a few basic tools, it’s very simple to do it yourself.

Recent findings suggest that the beauty of a cordless mower is that there’s less maintenance you need to perform. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t steps to take before storing it away for winter.

In a recent development, batteries are the lifeblood of a cordless mower, so you need to take care of them. Don’t leave them in the mower over winter, especially if you’re keeping it in an uninsulated shed that sees cold temperatures. Remove your batteries and charge them to between 40 and 60 percent. Check the charge level every two months or so, as lithium-ion batteries lose power over time. Partially recharge the batteries if they dip close to 20 percent or lower.

In a recent development, store your batteries in a cool, dark place such as a basement or insulated garage (but not near a furnace or heat source). For a riding mower that has a built-in battery you cannot remove, park it in a garage or at least a covered area. If stored in a place that gets below freezing, don’t leave it on a charger or try to recharge it, as some batteries (lithium-ion) should not be charged below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Get it to a warmer place or wait until a warmer day.

In a recent development, this isn’t much different from how you do it for a gas mower; just be careful if using water to do any cleaning, as this can potentially damage electrical components. Also, be sure to remove the batteries before you do any kind of cleaning on a cordless mower.

Again, this isn’t a different process than a gas mower; just make sure the batteries are removed first to avoid the chance of the mower starting up accidentally.

#88819. Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

📅 11 Jul 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family.
  • In a recent development, the batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake.
  • According to recent reports, the secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

In a recent development, the batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

According to recent reports, the secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

Sources indicate that no. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

Recent findings suggest that white and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

In a recent development, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Sources indicate that toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too swiftly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • Industry observers note that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Fresh York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

Industry observers note that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

Recent findings suggest that while there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Sources indicate that originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, noted that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

It has been revealed that part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she notes. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

It has been revealed that A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Recent findings suggest that spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, notes that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Industry observers note that delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

Sources indicate that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”.

Sources indicate that with which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Industry observers note that still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

Tech Report: Coffee May Be Changing Your Gut in Ways Scientists Are Only Beginning To Understand

💡 Key Takeaways
  • To find out what coffee might be doing deep in the gut, researchers sent a tiny sensor through the digestive tract.
  • Sources indicate that for many people, a morning cup of coffee does more than wake up the brain.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Copenhagen set out to investigate whether coffee drinking is linked to changes in gut function, particularly the muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive tract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To find out what coffee might be doing deep in the gut, researchers sent a tiny sensor through the digestive tract.

Sources indicate that for many people, a morning cup of coffee does more than wake up the brain. It also seems to get the digestive system moving, sometimes sending them straight to the bathroom. But what exactly happens deep inside the intestines after regular coffee consumption?

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Copenhagen set out to investigate whether coffee drinking is linked to changes in gut function, particularly the muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive tract. Understanding this connection could offer new insights into digestion and potentially point toward natural ways to relieve constipation.

According to recent reports, to see what was happening inside the digestive tract, the team asked Danish volunteers to swallow a small electronic capsule. As it traveled, the capsule recorded temperature, pH, and intestinal contractions, along with how long it took to pass through.

It has been revealed that over the eight-day study, the researchers compared volunteers who drank one to five cups of coffee on at least four days with those who drank coffee less often. The frequent coffee drinkers had a wider variety of gut microorganisms, consistent with earlier research linking coffee intake to differences in the makeup of gut bacteria.

It has been revealed that “But perhaps more importantly, frequent coffee consumption appears to affect the physiology of the gut itself, in other words, how the gut functions,” indicates first author Francesca Bucci, a PhD student in the University of Copenhagen’s Department of Nutrition, Exercise, and Sports. Earlier studies have linked moderate coffee intake to lower risks of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression, and several cancers. Its relationship with conditions inside the gut has received less attention.

Frequent coffee drinkers had a significantly lower pH in the small intestine, meaning it was more acidic. Higher coffee intake was also associated with more contractions in the colon.

“Contractions in the gut can support healthy digestion, help prevent constipation, and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition,” says Bucci.

According to recent reports, the implications of the lower pH are less clear. Digestive enzymes work best within particular pH ranges, so changes in acidity can affect how they break down food. The researchers still need to determine what the difference means for health.

It has been revealed that because participants followed their usual coffee habits, the study could only identify links. Other differences between the groups may have contributed to the findings. Senior author Henrik Munch Roager, an associate professor and research group leader in the same department, points to earlier evidence that coffee can influence digestion.

Sources indicate that “For example, we already know from other studies that coffee can influence a range of processes in the digestive system, including acid secretion in the stomach. So there are good reasons to believe that what we are seeing is not merely coincidence. Anecdotally, many people also report that coffee affects their digestion,” says Roager.

Roager proposes controlling how much coffee participants drink in a follow-up study. Comparing periods of high coffee intake with periods without coffee could help researchers pin down which changes are due to coffee itself.

According to recent reports, “A great many people struggle with constipation and irregular bowel movements. If we can understand how coffee affects digestion and intestinal contractions, it may be possible to use that knowledge to stimulate gut motility in a natural way. That would be extremely valuable,” claims Roager.

Reference: “Habitual coffee consumption is linked to differences in gut microbiota and gut physiology” by Francesca Bucci, Marie-Luise Puhlmann, Paula Rodriguez-Garcia, Xu Yujing, Jan Stanstrup, Jeroen Raes, Giorgia La Barbera, Nicola Procházková, Lars O. Dragsted, Martin F. Laursen and Henrik M. Roager, 15 September 2026, Gut Microbiology. DOI: 10.1016/j.gutmic.2026.100018.
