According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to backcountry safety, there’s no messing around. Serious adventure seekers know it’s best to prepare for their outdoor escapades—whether they’re heading deep into the wilderness or staying close to home. If not, you risk injury or worse. From a reliable fixed-blade knife to a solid pair of binoculars for scouting the trail ahead, there’s a whole slew of gear to keep you safe outdoors.

Used for decades, walkie-talkies are a lesser-talked-about gadget for hikers, campers, paddlers, bikers, skiers, and more heading into the wilderness. Yet this humble piece of equipment plays an crucial role in helping you communicate with colleagues, friends, and family when you’re on the go. They’re also a smart backup in an emergency and a way to monitor the weather in untamed landscapes and far-off places.

According to recent reports, today’s walkie-talkies haven’t changed all too much in look and feel from their early days. But they’re nothing like the cheap, toy versions we used as kids when exploring backyard “wilderness.” Modern features like NOAA weather alerts, VOX (hands-free operation), and app-connected features provide safeguards and peace of mind—especially in faraway places.

Our guide below covers what to keep in mind and how to choose a walkie-talkie for work, play, and emergencies—and offers a closer look at standout models worth your money.

Our evaluation process combined rigorous field testing across a wide variety of walkie-talkies in different environments with extensive research from trusted online sources. Meehan’s in-field testing for his best two-way radio picks ranged from trekking deep into the backcountry on hut trips to communicating seamlessly while mountain biking to traveling around a city.

Recognizing that walkie-talkies serve a wide audience, we also considered other scenarios where dependable communication is essential—on construction sites, inside expansive venues like convention centers, and across large retail operations.

With this breadth of uses in mind, we reviewed models spanning a range of functions and price points, carefully weighing usability, durability, range, features, and cost. For radios we couldn’t test directly, we reviewed trusted sources and compared specs. We also factored in real-world customer feedback, ensuring our final selections reflect not only expert insights but also everyday user experiences.

These Midland radios have proven reliable in the city and the mountains. The two-pack is a great value and includes advanced features like hands-free VOX and NOAA weather channel monitoring.

It's one of the most versatile walkie-talkies in terms of power options. As part of a two-pack, you get a charging cradle for each, but you can also charge the device with a micro-USB cable and, if you’re in the field for multiple days and run out of power, you can switch the battery pack out for a upcoming one or use three AA batteries to power it—though it is hard to get the cover off.

The radios are compatible with multiple accessories, like a hand-held mic-speaker or an earpiece-mic combo. The latter makes hands-free use even easier, like in a restaurant or store setting.

It has been revealed that the walkies boast 36 channels, some preconfigured for privacy. With privacy codes, it has 121 channels in total. The speaker and mic aren't as crisp as some other models, and the range isn’t as great as others.

But in the end, this relatively affordable set of walkies has an ideal feature set for most people.

Sources indicate that it shouldn’t surprise that a organization known for its smartphones, like the Razr+, would add smartphone-like features to its top-line walkie-talkies. That’s exactly what Motorola did with its 800-series Talkabout line.

It uses the Talkabout app for iOS and Android devices to enable features other walkie-talkies can’t, like letting you use the 800 series as a sort of smartphone modem when there’s no cell service.

The app also lets you send texts or share your location with others using an 800-series radio and the app. This feature is unavailable on most walkie-talkies, since they’re just two-way radios. It also supports smart pairing and connects to Bluetooth devices, like headphones or earbuds.

Sources indicate that beyond that, the 800 series Talkabout offers the features you’d expect in a good-quality walkie-talkie with access to the 22 FRS channels and 121 privacy codes. This T803 radio has advantages over the T800 (for example, a better weatherproof rating) and the T802, which doesn’t come with a rechargeable battery.

Most walkie-talkies on the market are waterproof, or at the very least water-resistant, since they’re meant for outdoor use. But you’ll find it harder to find a two-way radio that can actually float. That’s where Cobra's floating walkie-talkies stand out.

Recent findings suggest that built to IPX7 waterproof standards, this radio can survive full immersion underwater and is designed to float—ideal for situations like water sports, boating, paddling, skiing, and backcountry adventures. This walkie-talkie can handle dunkings and wet environments where communication is critical, and its orange rubber exterior makes it easy to spot in choppy surf or on snow-covered slopes.

Best for whitewater kayakers, stand-up paddle boarders, or even families enjoying a long weekend on the boat, it's a solid pick when you want to stay connected without worrying about waterlogging. You won’t have to worry about sinking or failing when wet. This durability is also ideal for backcountry skiers or climbers who deal with wet conditions daily.

Extra features like voice-activated transmission (aka hands-free talking) and the ability to replay missed radio calls also pack a punch. With its 37-mile range, NOAA weather alerts, and an impressive 2662 channel combinations, this Cobra radio is more than just waterproof—it’s an essential tool for adventurers heading into rugged, remote environments.

In the end, it’s hard to deny the Rocky Talkie Mountain Radio's capabilities compared to others made for outdoor adventure. It could easily have been our top pick, but since not everyone goes on multi-day backcountry trips, the Mountain Radio is likely overkill for most.

Founded in 2019, RockyTalkie is a newcomer to the scene, but it has nailed it with this 2-watt FRS radio with great range. Even in forested, mountainous areas, we could still easily communicate over miles. It also had one of the longest-lasting batteries, even in freezing weather.

Sources indicate that the Mountain Radio sports a really simple interface with just five buttons, and it’s easy to lock onto a channel. The radio also has a great speaker and microphone for transmitting and receiving calls and a bright green LED display that disappears when the radio isn’t actively transmitting or receiving.

We also appreciate the radio's rugged, rubberized outer shell and its two removable attachment points. The device uses carabiners rather than belt clips like most other two-way radios. That makes it easy to attach to just about anything—a harness, a belt loop, a backpack strap, a PFD, and more. The secondary attachment point uses smaller carabiners and a coiled leash, making it even harder to drop or lose.

The only thing we found lacking in the radio is that it can’t scan and play NOAA weather alerts, which would be very helpful in a backcountry setting with no access to cell service.

Industry observers note that the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio showcases backcountry endurance at its finest. It’s beefed-up, replaceable battery lasts up to six full days on a single charge. That’s nearly a week of reliable communication without scrambling for a power bank or solar panel to plug into while off-grid—making it one of the longest-lasting walkie-talkies in its class.

Industry observers note that this two-way radio also shines for its durability, with an IP67 waterproof and dustproof rating. It also includes NOAA weather alerts, dual-frequency monitoring, and up to 5 watts of transmitting power for extended range. An important note: you need a GMRS license to operate this radio legally in the field.

It has been revealed that while its design is compact, it’s heavier than many other walkie-talkies we tested. That said, for the peace of mind that comes with extended battery life and a durable design that tops our list for its rugged, waterproof build, you can’t go wrong with this radio.

Bottom line: the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt is our go-to choice for lasting power and rugged dependability.

While it’s technically not a walkie-talkie, the Garmin InReach Mini 2 deserves a spot in any serious communication roundup. For backcountry adventures where two-way communication is less frequent or a walkie-talkie just won’t cut it, this pocket-sized satellite device becomes a lifeline—especially when cell service and radio coverage fail.

According to recent reports, the InReach Mini 2 uses the Iridium satellite network to deliver global coverage wherever you roam. You can send two-way text messages, share GPS location, and trigger SOS alerts from literally anywhere in the world. This piece of tech is best described as a satellite phone stripped down to the essentials: sending and receiving messages without overcomplicating communications.

It weighs a mere 3.5 ounces, and its compact design lets you clip the sat-phone to your pack or strap, or slide it into your pocket. You can also sync the InReach Mini 2 with Garmin’s Earthmate app for easier texting if you have your phone with you on your adventures.

Another big selling point of this piece of gear over walkie-talkies is its 14-day lifespan—long enough for extended off-grid trips. Unlike FRS or GMRS walkie-talkies, which are limited by terrain and line-of-sight requirements, this communication device promises to keep you in touch with family and friends wherever your adventures take you. Even more importantly, it keeps you connected in an emergency.

In a recent development, while a walkie-talkie is a simple, handheld, portable two-way radio, not all are the same. Some are designed for indoor use, while others are meant for outdoor use. Some suit adventurers and sportspeople, while others offer features best suited to first responders. And, of course, some are designed for kids. When selecting the right two-way radios for your needs, there are plenty of factors to consider.

In a recent development, the basics are battery life, transmitting power or range, durability, weather/waterproofness, and remote capabilities. More advanced features include weather channels, VOX (voice-operated exchange, which is hands-free voice-activated transmission), access to NOAA weather channels, the ability to monitor multiple channels, privacy codes, headset ports, repeater channels, and NFC and Bluetooth connections.

Sources indicate that most walkie-talkies are Family Radio Service (FRS) units with 2 watts or less of broadcasting power. These need no license. Devices that have more than 2 watts of broadcasting power, up to 50 watts, are called General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) units.

Sources indicate that GMRS devices require an FCC license. However, as the folks at Rocky Talkie explain on their site, it’s pretty easy to get one online in the U.S. It costs $35 and is good for 10 years, covering everyone in your immediate family. The higher the wattage, the more transmitting power and range the walkie-talkie has, which generally means it uses more power and has a larger antenna. You can see that difference pretty clearly between the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio and the brand’s smaller 2-watt Mountain Radio.

It has been revealed that both types of units can broadcast on a range of channels, and each channel has wattage restrictions. Channels 1 through 7 can broadcast at up to 5 watts. Channels 8 through 14 can only broadcast at up to 0.5 watts. Channels 15 through 22 can broadcast at up to 50 watts, making them ideal for communications up to 30 miles apart in good conditions.

It has been revealed that some walkie-talkies can broadcast on other channels, but it's not recommended, as emergency and first responders may use them, and it’s illegal to broadcast on them. On the other hand, some Midland radios list “additional channels.” But in that case, they’re existing channels with pre-set privacy codes.

According to recent reports, speaking of, when using walkie talkies with a group of people it’s always important to check that everyone is on the same channel, and if using a private channel to reduce interference from others, that everyone is on the same privacy code. We’d also recommend locking the devices to that channel—unless you need to be on multiple channels or scanning channels.

Not all two-way radios are designed with the same level of user-friendliness and a simple interface. The interface plays a massive role in how easy the device is to use, especially when in the field with limited bandwidth for fidgeting with buttons and screen controls. Some radios keep things simple with large knobs and backlit buttons that let you seamlessly switch channels or adjust volume with a quick twist or tap—even while wearing gloves. Others rely on small digital menus that can be challenging to navigate, especially while on the go.

Recent findings suggest that and some advanced walkie-talkies even require setup, such as programming frequencies through a computer and cables. While this may give more control, it can intimidate newer two-way radio owners.

When comparing radios, pay attention to details like clearly marked buttons, backlit displays for night use, and easy setup processes. Features like one-touch scanning or memory recall can be great options when you need quick, efficient communication. Ultimately, the best radio delivers reliable performance without sacrificing user experience—especially when it matters most in the field.

In a recent development, most two-way radios use replaceable batteries, usually AA or AAA, rechargeable batteries, or sometimes can use either. Units with rechargeable batteries are often more expensive, but usually have good longevity for trail and backcountry use. Some units recharge in a cradle but ideally also have a port for charging via a DC or USB cable, allowing you to power up from a backup battery as needed. We’ve left units on overnight before and still had power in the morning, and some will go into a low-power mode when left on. The battery will last longer if you use the walkie less or use a lower wattage mode, but that will also reduce its transmitting and receiving range.

It has been revealed that obviously, you want your devices to last a long time, and walkie-talkies should endure for years and withstand knocks and drops. That's why most don’t have touchscreens or even glass screens. Most should be able to withstand minor spills or rain, but if you know you’ll be using them primarily in the water, like on a fishing boat or white-water rafting and kayaking, you’ll want a walkie-talkie that’s waterproof and carries an IP67 rating or higher. If you’re using walkies in the backcountry or on a job site, you’ll want two-way radios that are ruggedized—like the DeWalt 2-Watt Heavy-Duty Walkie-Talkie or Rocky Talkies—and can withstand drops better than some others.

In a recent development, walkie-talkies offer a few options for remote operation. Some will allow VOX or hands-free operation and are activated by your voice. Others have wired microphones and speakers that are handheld or worn on a lapel or shoulder strap. Others have an earpiece and microphone. Some modern walkie-talkies can actually pair with Bluetooth earpieces, also allowing for hands-free communication. This is great when wearing a motorcycle helmet or when a wire could get in the way of whatever you’re doing.

Some models have additional channel monitoring or communication capabilities, like operating on two frequencies at the same time. These are handy features, but using them will drain the battery faster while they’re on.

Walkie-talkies designed for outdoor use, for example, can monitor NOAA weather channels, giving you some insight into the weather and the conditions you may face while camping, driving off-road, hiking, or hunting that you otherwise wouldn’t be able to access.

Industry observers note that still others can communicate and monitor two channels at the same time. That could allow you to communicate with multiple teams at once. For instance, in a rescue situation, you could communicate with your friends on one channel and the local sheriff’s office or the search-and-rescue team on another without switching channels every time.

While all walkie-talkie channels are open to all users, some are generally used by certain groups and/or in certain areas. You can talk with local organizations to find out which channels they use and broadcast on.

In a recent development, to help people connect with like minds, some are encouraging what they call community channels. These help people in a local backcountry area communicate with each other. Rocky Talkie lists some active community channels for local areas. While these channels help in some situations, you also don’t want to communicate constantly on channels monitored by SAR or local sheriff’s offices, because you could interrupt emergency operations.

Walkie-talkies come in a wide range of prices, and more expensive models often offer more benefits and features. So, while you can get a serviceable pair for about $30-$35, they won’t have much range or additional features. For a top-tier single walkie-talkie with multi-channel monitoring, high wattage and range, and water- and shock-proofing, you can expect to pay over $150 per unit.

Range is one of the biggest selling points for walkie-talkies, but it’s also one of the most misunderstood. Sure, the box may say “up to 35 miles of range.” That’s only if conditions are near-perfect—think one person on a mountain peak and another down in a valley, with nothing but clear air between them. In reality, terrain, obstructions, severe weather (like a snowstorm), and more can drastically cut that range. Dense forest, rocky canyons, massive hills, and buildings can shrink that range even more.

Most consumer FRS models perform best up to five miles, depending on the terrain. For most outdoor adventures, a reliable one-to-five-mile range is typical and usually enough to keep track of groups across rivers, campsites, or trails. GMRS radios, which we mentioned require a license, can stretch much further than five miles, especially when paired with repeaters.

Our recommendation: Shop for a walkie-talkie model and range based on realistic expectations for your use case, not the maximum range advertised in the brand’s marketing.

It depends! How often and for how long do you initiative to use your radio? Are you looking for a basic radio or one built to perform off-grid? Battery life depends most on design and how often you use it. Most walkie-talkies advertise a battery lifespan of eight to 20 hours of runtime, but those numbers assume moderate to infrequent use. Continuous transmission drains the battery much faster than standby mode.

Industry observers note that for shorter day hikes and quick outings, you won’t have to worry much about your radio lasting more than a single charge. On longer excursions, opt for a walkie-talkie that can be charged via USB-C with an external battery pack, or that uses AA or AAA batteries. Simply put: Don’t trust what the packaging indicates. Instead, consider how long you proposal to use the two-way radio and whether you’ll have a chance to recharge partway through a long adventure.

Many modern two-way radios offer more than basic push-to-talk functionality. NOAA weather alerts are especially helpful for backcountry safety, providing real-time updates on weather patterns and severe storms heading your way.

Another feature to look for is VOX—voice-activated transmission—which enables hands-free use. Paddlers, bikers, and skiers are prime candidates for VOX-equipped walkie-talkies when devices aren’t always easy to grab while in motion.

Other bonus features to look for include the ability to scan multiple channels, privacy codes to reduce interference from strangers, and built-in flashlights and SOS alarm signaling in emergencies.

Industry observers note that for simple day-hiking trail use or communicating with your family across the campground, simple models will work just fine. But on bigger adventures like backpacking into the wilderness and remote paddling, investing in a two-way radio with all the bells and whistles gives you peace of mind and the right tools when conditions are worse than expected.

Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.
  • For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step.
  • Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

Sources indicate that during angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the new analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

In a recent development, the central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

According to recent reports, “When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

Sources indicate that “We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”.

Recent findings suggest that these results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

According to recent reports, although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a newly introduced randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

The research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala noted considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

In a recent development, reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

It has been revealed that there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

According to recent reports, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

According to recent reports, making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a big party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with significant flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Sources indicate that back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

It has been revealed that the recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe.
  • But the CMB has also changed over time with the expansion of the Universe.
  • According to recent reports, two space telescopes have played vital roles in mapping the CMB: the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probee (WMAP), and the Planck satellite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe. It dates back to the recombination epoch, when photons could first travel freely through the cosmos. The CMB is like a snapshot of the state of energy and matter about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

But the CMB has also changed over time with the expansion of the Universe. As the Universe has expanded, the CMB has been stretched into microwave wavelengths that we can't see. That's why, despite containing the overwhelming majority of the Universe's photons, we can't see it without the help of telescopes.

According to recent reports, two space telescopes have played vital roles in mapping the CMB: the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probee (WMAP), and the Planck satellite. They were both up above the obscuring effect of Earth's atmosphere, which is the main obstacle to observing the CMB. The CMB is nearly uniform, but not quite. It has tiny irregularities that cosmologist have mapped in increasing detail. These small temperature inhomogeneities can reveal a lot about the Universe and the Major Bang.

This is the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe's heat map of temperature fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background. (Credit : NASA / WMAP Science Team).

Industry observers note that but there's also another way of studying the CMB. The South Pole Telescope is a 10-meter radio telescope in Antarctica that takes advantage of a small atmospheric window to observe part of the CMB. It's also in a designated "radio-quiet zone." It's credited with discovering a upcoming feature of the CMB called the B-mode polarization. Gravitational lensing by intervening matter like galaxy clusters created this B-mode polarization. That proved that the CMB can hold evidence of gravitatonal effects.

Sources indicate that that was a significant deal because the polarization had been predicted decades earlier. The CMB's polarization is almost perfectly uniform. But almost isn't completely, and there are tiny variations in the B-mode polarity. In this case, these tiny changes were created by intervening matter.

The CMB's polarization was first detected in 2002, and that was a massive accomplishment. John Carlstrom from the University of Chicago led the collaboration that detected it, and he is now the director of the South Pole Telescope. âWe were sitting around with a small team, looking at our computer. There were peaks and wiggles, just as predicted,â Carlstrom said. âWe were just staring at it and it was just phenomenal.â.

It has been revealed that the South Pole Telescope hard at work during the long polar night. Image Credit: Report of the U.S. Antarctic Program Blue Ribbon Panel - More and Better Science in Antarctica Through Increased Logistical Effectiveness, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/25790806.

Recent findings suggest that âItâs one of the ways that we can understand gravity at these very extreme scales,â stated Kimmy Wu, an assistant professor at the California Institute of Technology, one of the institutions involved in the south pole observations. âThe fact that there could be primordial gravitational waves means that at the early fraction of a second when the universe was quantum fluctuations, gravity worked.â.

Recent findings suggest that quantum gravity can only be detected in this very early fraction of a second. It's beyond the capabilities of supercolliders to examine, and these tiny waves are the only way to observe quantum gravity. If quantum gravity can be detected in the very first moments of the Universe, then it can help physicists bridge the gap between General Relativity, which describes things on a massive scale, and quantum physics, which describes things on a tiny scale. So finding these tiny primordial gravitational waves brings us closer to a unified theory of how everything works. That would be nice; just ask any physicist.

In a recent development, this graphic helps explain the complicated problem facing physicists. If they can detect B-mode polarization in the CMB, it's evidence that quantum fluctuations generated primordial gravitational waves. Image Credit: By Original: DrbogdanâVector: Yinweichen - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31825049.

Recent findings suggest that but as stated earlier, these first B-mode detections were due to gravitational lensing, not quantum gravity. The next natural question was, can the B-mode contain evidence of primordial, quantum gravity? A fresh instrument was needed to find out.

Next to the South Pole Telescope is the Background Imaging of Cosmic Extragalactic Polarization (BICEP) array. BICEP was built to measure the B-mode polarization of the CMB that come directly from quantum gravity. The current iteration of BICEP is the fifth, and overall, it's been working since 2006.

Recent findings suggest that if BICEP can detect these tiny gravitational ripples from the Universe's very beginnings, then our understanding of the tiniest workings of the Universe will take shape. It would provide the most robust evidence for inflation and Big Bang cosmology.

Members of the BICEP team in front of BICEP. The array is articulated and sits inside a specially designed protective blue windproof and thermally insulated cover. Image Credit: BICEP Array.

âIf we could detect these B-modes robustly, then itâs bulletproof,â said Lindsey Bleem, a physicist at DOEâs Argonne National Laboratory who worked at the South Pole in 2008 and 2014.

If they can rule out these B-modes, then physicists need to revise models of inflation or work on other ones. Either way, it's progress.

But there's another mode of CMB polarization called E-mode. They are both weaker and harder to detect than temperature fluctuations in the CMB. In fact, the E-mode is only one-tenth as strong as the temperature fluctuations, and the B-mode is even weaker.

Industry observers note that âWe are here in the business of making a super, super precise measurement. This is basically a few nanokelvin on top of the 2.725 [degrees] of the CMB,â mentioned Zeeshan Ahmed, associate professor at Stanford University and researcher at DOEâs SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory.

This image shows an illustration of the Planck satellite over the satellite's map of the CMB. It's work was an improvement of the WMAP's map. Image Credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration - D. Ducros.

Industry observers note that when measuring something so faint, interference becomes a major problem. Other radiation sources can pollute signals, the Milky Way's dust can add its own polarization, and some E-modes can transform into B-modes. It all adds up to one of the most complicated challenges in science.

In a recent development, but the SPT and BICEP each have different strengths, and by working together, scientists think they can find a way forward. âItâs like a marriage,â said Bleem. âBICEP has the intense sensitivity at large scales and SPT can make these wonderful gravitational lensing maps, without which BICEP would be completely limited by the systematics. Together, they can achieve the targeted goals.â.

Other telescopes like Herschel and Planck contribute too, by sorting out and mapping sources of interference in the signal that can lense the E-mode signal.

Recent findings suggest that âIf there is a signal, you should be able to see that in both places,â noted Wu. âThese are excellent ways to really check whether a claim of detection is substantiated.â.

Recent findings suggest that that was an important step. It provided a way to determine what E-modes had been warped by gravity to appear like B-modes. That was a potential way through the mess.

âBeing able to measure that signal for the first time â¦ was very exciting,â recalled Carlstrom.

It has been revealed that in 2014, the BICEP2 team presented a paper to their peers showing that they had detected B-mode polarization indicating a gravitational wave signal from inflation. Their excitement was short-lived though. Subsequent examination and new data from other researchers showed that the signal could be attributed to the Milky Way's problematic dust.

This image illustrates how the Milky Way's dust can polarize the CMB. Image Credit: ESA.

âWe dialed up our skepticism on these things in the last ten years,â noted Ahmed, who works on the BICEP Array. âIf latest data is coming in and it can be co-analyzed with ours, we would love that.â.

It has been revealed that work continues on this complicated problem, and the potential payoff is so monumental that setbacks aren't deterring the researchers. They continue to work on eliminating sources of uncertainty in the data.

Sources indicate that they're getting a better handle on how gravitational lensing affects data and how to understand what mode of polarization they're sensing. They're improving instrument precision and eliminating more noise. Upcoming improvements to both the South Pole Telescope and BICEP will drive further progress.

Industry observers note that for now, there's no unambiguous detection of primordial gravitational waves. But work continues in the extreme conditions at the bottom of the world, with ever-improving telescopes and the apparent unbreakable will of the dedicated researchers.

âIt is really rewarding to see the SPT. When I started working on it, it was just a proposal â we hadnât built the telescope yet,â stated Benson. âThe fact that we can still do cutting-edge science with it and sustaining it over 20 years has been really satisfying.â.

Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find Newly introduced Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.
  • It has been revealed that A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years.
  • It has been revealed that for example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

It has been revealed that A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a newly introduced Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

It has been revealed that for example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

The method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” indicates Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

In a recent development, researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Sources indicate that using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that the approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” says Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very crucial in treatment decisions.”.

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

According to recent reports, “Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” states Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”.

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not right now recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292.

#88787. Black Holes and Their Mysterious Bright Structures Explained

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1512 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

Black Holes and Their Mysterious Bright Structures Explained

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that astrophysical jets launched from black holes aren't shy.
  • Recent findings suggest that supermassive black holes (SMBH) emit the largest astrophysical jets, and they come from active galactic nuclei (AGN) which are SMBH that are actively accreting material.
  • These jets are impossible to ignore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that astrophysical jets launched from black holes aren't shy. They announce their presence with enormous blasts of energy that extend extreme distances into space. They're the most long-lasting and luminous sources of electromagnetic energy in the Universe.

Recent findings suggest that supermassive black holes (SMBH) emit the largest astrophysical jets, and they come from active galactic nuclei (AGN) which are SMBH that are actively accreting material. As material gathers in an accretion disk around a SMBH, it rotates and heats up. Some of the material is ejected out of the black hole in the powerful jets.

These jets are impossible to ignore. No astrophysicist could feign their interest. Exactly how these powerful expressions of cosmic energy are created isn't clear, though some things are known.

In a recent development, astrophysicists know that they're powered by a SMBH's rotational energy and their extremely powerful magnetic fields. They know that they move at relativistic speeds. And they know that they can inject gigantic amounts of energy into the intergalactic medium, heating up gas and introducing turbulence, two things that act against star formation.

One thing that puzzles researchers is how the different regions in a black hole jet have different brightnesses. The expectation is that the center of the jets would be brightest, because this is where energy is most concentrated. But when researchers examine the jets coming from the SMBH in Centaurus A, the closest radio galaxy to Earth, that's not what they see.

In a recent development, since it's so close and so bright, Centaurus A is one of those natural laboratories for extreme physics that makes astrophysicists' eyes light up. They've been observing the jets in Centaurus A in detail for many years. Observations with the Event Horizon Telescope spanning a decade have revealed that its jets are brighter at their edges than in their centers, in a phenomenon called limb brightening. Why is that?

In a recent development, new research in Astronomy and Astrophysics has an explanation. It's titled "Probing anisotropic particle acceleration and limb brightening in Centaurus Aâs jet." The lead author is Felix Glaser, Master's student at the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg in Germany.

"Relativistic jets are among the most fascinating phenomena in the universe, and recent high-resolution very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations, including the Global mm-VLBI Array and the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), are able to resolve their structure close to their launching site," the authors write. The combined observations show the black holes with brighter limbs are not only found in Centaurus A, but in M 87 and 3C 84, too.

This image indicates four different looks at the central region of M 87. The top image from the Hubble is in visible light. The other three are all in polarised light. The lines mark the orientation of polarisation, which is related to the magnetic field in the regions imaged. Though the researchers focused on Centaurus A, this image highlights how magnetic fields and polarity influence astrophysical jets. Image Credit: EHT Collaboration; ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), Goddi et al.; NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); VLBA (NRAO), Kravchenko et al.; J. C. Algaba, I. MartÃ­-Vidal.

Each of these three galaxies are different from one another, making it difficult to understand the cause of their limb brightening. "Therefore, as a pilot study, we aimed to model the EHT observations of Cen A," the authors explain. It's the closest, so that makes sense.

This is a composite image of Centaurus A, with the individual images and their wavelenghts on the right. The image is from the Hubble (visible), Chandra (X-ray), Spitzer (infrared), and the Very Large Array (radio). Image Credit: NASA, CXC, SAO, Astrophotography by Rolf Olsen, NASA-JPL, Caltech, NRAO, AUI, NSF, UOH, M. Hardcastle.

The researchers performed a magnetohydrodynamic simulation of an accreting supermassive black hole and how it released it jets to observe the plasma dynamics involved. Since these jets are relativistic, the simulation included general relativistic effects. They also adjusted their simulation to match the properties of Centaurus A. "In order to match our model to the EHT observations, we adjust several free parameters..." the authors write, including black hole mass and the viewing angle.

The simulation successfully mimicked the recent observations of Centaurus A with the EHT.

"Our results demonstrate that the edge-brightening observed in Cen A can be naturally reproduced by an anisotropic particle distribution," the researchers write.

That means that the electrons emitted in the jets aren't distributed evenly over pitch angles. Pitch angles are the difference between the magnetic field and each electron's velocity. This is where synchrotron radiation enters the picture. Synchrotron radiation is when particles are forced to follow the curve of a magnetic field.

In a recent development, the emission of synchrotron radiation is strongly dependent on the pitch angle. So as a result, the observed brightness of the radiation changes depending on the viewing angle of the magnetic field the particles are forced to follow.

Industry observers note that this figure from the research indicates the synthetic polarized intensity images of our Cen A model at four representative frequencies: 86 GHz (panel A), 230 GHz (panel B), 680 GHz (panel C), and 3 THz (panel D). Each one zooms in closer and shows more detail in the model. Image Credit: Glaser et al. 2026.

According to recent reports, âWhat is truly amazing is that microscopic plasma effects can shape structures on vastly larger scales,â noted Dr. Christian Fromm, leader of the Computational Astrophysics Group. âFuture observations will reveal even more of these plasma signatures, making it increasingly notable to include realistic plasma physics in our models already today and to further investigate the highly nonlinear effects of relativistic plasma.â.

This figure highlights how microscopic plasma effects can shape the large-scale structure of black hole jets. The hot accretion flow surrounding the supermassive black hole is shown in red, the relativistic jets in blue, and the magnetic field structure by gray helical field lines. Colored particles and arrows illustrate the motion of accelerated particles along the jet. Top right: The Event Horizon Telescope image of the inner jet of Centaurus A at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. Bottom right: The synthetic EHT observation generated from the fresh plasma-informed model. (Image Credit: Christian M. Fromm, Janssen et al. 2021 and Glaser et al. 2026).

According to recent reports, âCen A is our closest window into the physics of relativistic jets,â said lead author Glaser. âThe fact that our plasma-informed model reproduces the observed edge brightening suggests that we are capturing an crucial piece of the underlying physics. These processes may not be unique to Cen A, but could be common in relativistic jets throughout the Universe.â.

Sources indicate that this study makes real progress in understanding the details of astrophysical jets, and how they exhibit things like limb brightening. It links the small scale of plasma physics with the jets and their characteristics. It's all because of a focused, multi-disciplinary effort.

âBy bringing together expertise in high-resolution observations, numerical simulations, and plasma physics, we are making progress toward understanding how black holes launch powerful jets and how these jets produce the radiation we observe. The upcoming study is an excellent example of this approach,â said Fromm.

In a recent development, new telescopes are coming online that will take this work even further. The Square Kilometre Array will be the world's largest and highest-resolution radio telescope when it comes online in 2027. Updates to the Very Large Array will also drive progress when they're completed in 2031.

According to recent reports, this work may affect more than our understanding of black hole jets. On a detailed plasma physics level, there are similarities between the jets and fusion. If we ever have a functioning fusion reactor, it will involve extremely powerful artificial magnets to generate powerful fields that confine the plasma.

According to recent reports, this illustration reveals some of the "D"-shaped toroidal field magnets in the ITER international nuclear fusion research and engineering project being built in France. Each magnet weighs 330 tons, and their job is to confine the plasma inside ITER's vacuum vessel. Lessons learned by studying plasma physics in black hole jets are applicable to fusion reactors. Image Credit: ITER Consortium.

These insights not only help us understand the Universe, but may also contribute to the development of future fusion energy.â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

In a recent development, in the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

It has been revealed that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

It has been revealed that I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for Fresh Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Sources indicate that as the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Sources indicate that there are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

Latest Update: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a newly introduced set of patients.
  • Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a newly introduced set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up newly introduced versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Sources indicate that now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, says Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

According to recent reports, in the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most crucial is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Sources indicate that mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

Industry observers note that “It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” indicates Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”.

In a recent development, mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and consumers are happy to tweak.

According to recent reports, as the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann indicates, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

In a recent development, when people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving consumers in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman says.

Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Now, it’s a different story, Sethi says.

According to recent reports, patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she states. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

In July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman states. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will quickly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she claims. “I think it’s important to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • However, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Significant Bang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. These galaxies were bright and red - earning them the nickname Little Red Dots (LRDs) - and far more abundant than cosmological models predicted. Scientists theorized that these were early quasars, galaxies with active galactic nuclei (AGNs) powered by the "seeds" that would grow to become supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

However, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Significant Bang. This led scientists to consider various theories, compact collections of stars, "dusty" galaxies, supermassive stars, and "black hole stars." While the more recent Direct Collapse Black Holes (DCBHs) theory offered the most compelling argument to date, latest simulations by an international team of astronomers indicate that they may be the remnants of collapsed supermassive primordial stars.

Industry observers note that the study was led by Dr. Daniel Whalen from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation. His colleagues included researchers from United Arab Emirates University, the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the Institute for Astronomy and Royal Observatory at the University of Edinburgh, and the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA). The paper detailing their findings was published in the The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The little red dots could represent galaxies in an evolutionary phase predating the luminous quasar phase. Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/ISTA)/ETH Zurich/NAOJ.

Previous attempts to explain the rapid formation, abundance, and spectral characteristics of LRDs all suffered from the same issue. While each explained some characteristics, none could account for everything the JWST revealed in its deep field surveys. Then came the DCBHs theory, which argues that SMBH seeds formed directly from massive clouds of cold gas. While this theory did fit Webb's observations nicely, it still faces numerous theoretical and environmental challenges.

Recent findings suggest that for starters, the core premise of the DCBH theory is that a massive cloud of cold gas could collapse under its own gravity. However, gas tends to fragment into smaller clouds as it cools, leading to a cluster of primordial (Population III) stars instead of a black hole seed. To prevent fragmentation, the gas cloud must remain hot, requiring a very specific amount of Lyman-Werner (LW) radiation from a synchronized star-forming galaxy in its vicinity to destroy the main coolant - i.e., molecular hydrogen (Hâ).

This raises additional problems, including the self-shielding nature of molecular hydrogen. As a gas cloud becomes increasingly dense, its outer layers absorb the LW radiation, shielding the inner core. This means that the critical amount of radiation required to suppress cooling across the entire cloud would be much higher. Even if the SMBH seed did manage to form, the radiative pressure it would emit (plus mechanical feedback from the disk and jets) would slow the accretion rate, significantly slowing further growth.

Whalen and his team found another explanation borne out by advanced cosmological simulations. As he said in a University of Portsmouth press release:.

LRDs have been one of the most surprising discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope. They are compact, only a few hundred light-years across, but are as bright as much larger galaxies, and their unusual V-shaped spectra have defied the usual astrophysical explanations. Their lack of detectable X-ray and radio emissions has left astronomers struggling to explain what they are.

It has been revealed that artist's impression of a galaxy forming stars within powerful outflows of material blasted out from supermassive black holes at its core. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser.

Based on their simulations, the team produced a model showing that LRDs are most likely galaxies with AGN powered by massive black holes that formed through the collapse of supermassive primordial stars. What's more, their model suggests that the black holes are largely concealed by dense, massive discs of the gas that created them. These gaseous envelopes trap high-energy X-rays while allowing some visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light to escape, which fits with the unusual light signatures detected by the JWST.

It has been revealed that the simulations also explain another long-standing mystery about LRDs: that a large cluster of stars in the disks of these small galaxies produces the blue part of the spectrum Webb observed. These disks, according to the models, contain around 100 million stars densely packed into regions measuring only 500 light-years in diameter, matching what astronomers observed in LRDs. Based on the available data, the team further concludes the black holes at the center of these primordial galaxies are only about 10 million Solar masses.

This is a few orders of magnitude less than previous estimates, which indicated a maximum of 100 million Solar masses. While this research is unlikely to be the final word on the nature of LRDs, it offers what is (to date) the most fitting explanation that matches the observations. "What makes this discovery so exciting is that we may be witnessing the birth of the first supermassive black holes," stated Whalen. "For decades, simulations have predicted that these objects should exist, and now the James Webb Space Telescope may finally be allowing us to see them.".

Further Reading: University of Portsmouth, The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Scientists Develop Latest Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone
